items.title: Checking work email on the commute in seemed to help people start the day; doing it on the way home brought work into the house
items.angle: Same habit, opposite effect depending on direction. Workers who used work tech on the way in detached from home and got into work faster. Doing it on the way home was linked to more work-to-home conflict.
items.why_now: 6 days online. It's a relatable work finding for the Friday issue.
items.is_it_real: Thin to moderate. 149 employees tracked over 10 workdays, all self-reported. One hypothesized path (evening conflict hurting next-day engagement) was not significant. Daily associations can't rule out reverse causation. The caveat fits in a clause.

studies.caveats: All measures are self-reported, including engagement speed; one key hypothesized path (work-to-home conflict predicting next-day engagement speed) was not significant; N=149 over a short 10-day window; daily within-person associations cannot fully rule out reverse causation or unmeasured daily events; country and occupational context not specified in the abstract.

items.title: New job? Focusing only on mastering the tasks was the worst way to settle in over 18 months; learning the people and the place mattered too
items.angle: The instinct to prove yourself by nailing the work alone was the onboarding path tied to the worst outcomes among 932 new hires. People who also invested in their team and the wider organization did better.
items.why_now: About 5 days online (date not verified). It's useful advice for anyone starting a job.
items.is_it_real: Thin to moderate. 932 newcomers over 18 months, but observational. The profile analysis is sensitive to modeling choices, and outcomes appear to be self-reported. The digest's fact-check says 'task-only is worst' matches the abstract, but the specific claims about exhaustion and turnover go slightly beyond it. Stick to 'fared worst' unless the paper confirms more. The online date needs confirming.

studies.caveats: Observational longitudinal design, so profile membership is associated with, not proven to cause, outcomes; outcomes appear to be self-reported, including performance; profile analyses are sensitive to modeling choices; sample composition and country context are not detailed in the abstract.

items.title: A nerve-silencing knee injection for arthritis pain did no better than placebo over a full year, and caused more side effects
items.angle: RTX-GRT7039 (resiniferatoxin), a once-promising non-opioid option for knee osteoarthritis, failed its Phase 3 trial at 12, 26 and 52 weeks. Both groups improved a lot, which says something about how much of injection relief is placebo.
items.why_now: 7 days online. It's a clean negative Phase 3 result in a condition millions of older adults live with.
items.is_it_real: Strong for what it tests: a 469-person double-blind randomized trial over 52 weeks, with an effect over placebo of -0.11 WOMAC points (p=0.569). Adverse events were 62.8% vs 48.3%. Grünenthal funded it. The sponsor may have announced topline results earlier, so check before calling it new.

studies.caveats: industry funding [Grünenthal GmbH], no age breakdown reported, short follow-up relative to chronic disease course

items.title: Two years after the first over-the-counter birth control pill launched, 4 of 344 young Latine adults in a California farm region had used it
items.angle: Putting Opill on the shelf didn't mean people knew about it. Awareness rose only from 11% to 19%. Those who knew tended to get sexual health information from doctors, which suggests outreach and trusted messengers are the missing step.
items.why_now: 2 days online. Contraception access is in the news again (the post-Dobbs KFF knowledge-gap item is already queued).
items.is_it_real: Thin but honest. A prospective cohort of 344 people in one agricultural California community, with self-reported use. It isn't national, so frame it as one community.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 for some subgroups; total N=344), single-center, observational design, self-reported outcomes, narrow to one agricultural California community

items.title: College athletes told to aim for 10 hours of sleep a night ended up sleeping about 7.5, the same as before
items.angle: 'Just sleep more' is advice that's hard to follow. When 50 Division I athletes were told to target 10 hours, total sleep didn't rise (7.63 to 7.51 hours), though bedtimes got a little more regular. This complicates the much-repeated idea that elite athletes bank sleep for performance.
items.why_now: 1 day online. It pairs with this week's daylight-saving 'fall back' sleep searches.
items.is_it_real: Thin. Small (n=50), offseason, a two-week intervention measured by WHOOP wristbands, and WHOOP funded the study. It tests whether people can extend sleep, not whether extending it helps performance.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), elite athlete sample (may not generalize), short follow-up, single-center, industry funding [WHOOP Inc.]

items.title: HRT use in Denmark doubled after a decade at record lows, and vaginal estrogen use has more than doubled since 1999
items.angle: National sales data show systemic hormone therapy among women 45 to 64 fell from 20% in 2001 to 4% in 2013 and is back to 8% in 2025, still well under half the pre-WHI peak. The take: a comeback, but a slow one.
items.why_now: 3 days online. 'New hormone therapy patch' is exploding in searches this week. It is also nearly a year since the FDA moved to drop the boxed warning on menopause HRT (announced November 2025; confirm the current label status before citing it).
items.is_it_real: Moderate for what it is. These are national pharmacy sales, which don't show actual use or why it was prescribed. It is Denmark only, so it can't stand in for US use.

studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (Denmark), sales data may not reflect actual use or clinical indication

items.title: Recess before lunch gets kids eating more of their school lunch, two studies find, though in one it only moved the fruit
items.angle: In Anchorage, schools with recess first and longer lunch and recess periods saw kids eat more entrées, milk, fruit and vegetables. In Virginia, recess first nudged up fruit only and didn't change overall diet quality. That's a cheap scheduling fix with a modest, real effect.
items.why_now: Both are 1 to 2 days online in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. 'Reverse recess' is a recurring school-policy topic.
items.is_it_real: Moderate taken together, thin apart. Both are cross-sectional plate-waste studies (2,963 trays in Anchorage, 2,524 in Virginia), and each covers one region. The Virginia data is from a single day in 2019-2020. Neither shows causation.

studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
studies.caveats: observational design, cross-sectional, single-region (Anchorage, Alaska), post-test only, no sex-disaggregated data

studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
studies.caveats: observational design, cross-sectional, secondary analysis, single-day assessment, Virginia-only schools, no sex-disaggregated data

items.title: Fall back week: evening workouts didn't wreck older adults' sleep, and morning light and movement nudge your body clock earlier
items.angle: Two quick receipts for the clock change. In a small Dutch crossover trial of insomniacs aged 60 to 80, the time of day they exercised made no difference to insomnia, though morning activity shifted the middle of their sleep about 19 minutes earlier. In a separate 182-worker experiment, 30 minutes of bright blue light at breakfast improved that night's sleep and next-day alertness.
items.why_now: Clocks fall back Nov 1, and 'daylight saving time' and 'circadian depression' are both rising in Trend Desk. Friday's issue lands two days before the change.
items.is_it_real: Both are small and short. The exercise trial had 31 people with usable sleep data over two-week periods, insomnia improved even in the inactive period, and a co-author's company was paid for the melatonin assays. The light study ran for two weeks, its work outcomes were self-reported, and the age and sleep-problem subgroups were exploratory. Neither study is enough for a pitch, but they're fine as a hedged item.

studies.caveats: Small N (31 participants with sleep data); short two-week intervention periods; single center in the Netherlands; subjective sleep quality was self-reported via app; insomnia scores improved in the inactive period too, suggesting participation effects; a co-author's company received payment for the melatonin assessments.

Two-week time horizon; work outcomes were self-reported by the same participants; the sleep-alertness-performance chain is a mediation model within an experiment, not separately manipulated; moderation findings (age, prior sleep problems) were exploratory.

items.title: Is your baby sleeping through the night? A wrist tracker says 91% of 6-month-olds are; mothers' diaries say 40%
items.angle: The 'sleeping through the night' milestone depends on how you measure it. By actigraphy, 91% of babies qualified; by diary, 40%. Mothers judged it by the longest unbroken stretch, which is something to keep in mind before trusting a baby sleep tracker or comparing notes in a parenting group.
items.why_now: Online for 1 day (verified), not covered. Baby sleep trackers and sleep-milestone advice get a lot of online attention.
items.is_it_real: A small study: 56 mothers at one center (McGill), 6-month-olds only. It's a measurement comparison, not a finding about how babies should sleep.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, narrow age range (6 months only), observational design

items.title: Using fewer restraints on older ventilated ICU patients was as safe and got them off the ventilator sooner
items.angle: Something families can ask about: in a randomized trial of 485 ventilated sepsis patients aged 65 and older, restraining them only when severely agitated didn't increase deaths, self-extubation or sedative use. It also meant a little more time off the ventilator and out of a coma.
items.why_now: Online for 1 day (verified), not covered.
items.is_it_real: A randomized trial at five Chinese ICUs. It was open-label, the main outcome (days alive without delirium or coma) didn't differ, and the benefits were under a day. ICU practice varies by country.

studies.caveats: Open-label design (staff knew group assignment); conducted entirely in Chinese ICUs, so practice patterns may not match other countries; benefits were real but modest in absolute terms (under a day); the authors themselves note the safety of restraint minimization needs further evaluation.

items.title: Slower thinking, not forgetting, is the first sign of the 'white matter changes' on so many older adults' MRIs
items.angle: If a scan report mentions white matter hyperintensities, a 24-study analysis maps what tends to change and in what order: processing speed first, even with mild changes; planning and judgment at moderate stages; memory mostly at severe stages; general intelligence not at all.
items.why_now: 'Slow cognitive processing in conversation' is exploding in Trend Desk searches. Online today (verified).
items.is_it_real: A meta-analysis of observational studies (16 had enough data to pool) with large unexplained differences between them. It can't show cause and covers white matter changes only.

studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of observational studies — cannot establish causation; substantial unexplained heterogeneity across studies; attention and working memory estimates were based on too few studies to reach significance; focused almost entirely on white matter hyperintensities rather than other small-vessel pathologies.

items.title: Cold snaps raise the risk of a COPD flare-up about two weeks later; heat waves do it the same day
items.angle: A useful timing fact for winter: after cold weather, COPD flare risk peaked 14 to 18 days later, which is long enough that patients rarely connect the two. Heat risk peaked within 24 hours. The link was stronger in older adults, men and smokers.
items.why_now: Winter is starting. Online for 7 days (verified), not covered.
items.is_it_real: A case-crossover study of 5,981 flare-ups in Korean national insurance data. Relative risks were modest (1.23 for cold, 1.06 for heat), it covers one country, and it's observational.

studies.caveats: observational design, single-country cohort (South Korea), surrogate endpoints only

items.title: A probiotic sold as an iron booster added nothing to iron pills for anemia in a placebo-controlled trial
items.angle: A null result that saves money: in a double-blind trial of 200 adults aged 60+ with anemia, adding a 30-billion-CFU probiotic to iron-folic acid didn't raise hemoglobin any more than iron plus placebo did over 12 weeks. Iron stores actually rose more on placebo.
items.why_now: Online for 2 days (verified). Supplements marketed for gut health and absorption are everywhere.
items.is_it_real: A well-designed RCT, but in one community in India with one probiotic formula over 12 weeks. 16 of 200 dropped out (handled with last-value-carried-forward), and baseline microbiomes differed between groups. It doesn't rule out every probiotic strain.

studies.caveats: Single trial conducted in one region of India in a community cohort, so findings may not generalize to all older populations or to other probiotic formulations and doses; 12-week follow-up is short; 16 of 200 participants did not complete follow-up and missing values were imputed by last observation carried forward; baseline gut microbiome diversity differed between groups.

items.title: An online brain-training game meant to make junk food less tempting didn't change what 512 people ordered for dinner
items.angle: A pre-registered trial tested 'inhibitory control training,' the tap-to-resist games pitched as a craving fix. The trained group ordered 1,270 calories versus 1,287 in the control group, and no fewer of them picked pizza.
items.why_now: Online for 6 days (verified). Craving-control apps keep getting pitched.
items.is_it_real: Randomized and pre-registered with 512 UK adults, but the orders were hypothetical on a mock delivery site, not real purchases, and training done at home is hard to control.

studies.caveats: hypothetical food ordering (not real purchases), online delivery limits intervention fidelity, UK-based sample

items.title: Reviews from paid 'premium members' are rosier and less useful, according to 153,000 JD.com reviews
items.angle: A shopping tip with a hook: the badged loyalty-member rave tends to rate higher, run more emotional and get fewer helpful votes. The badge makes readers trust it more, but not enough to make up for content that says less.
items.why_now: Online for 2 days (verified). Holiday shopping season is about to start, and paid memberships like Prime and Walmart+ are everywhere.
items.is_it_real: The review data come from one Chinese platform and are correlational. Members choose to join, so happier customers may both sign up and rate higher. The follow-up experiments were lab-based. Helpfulness is measured by readers' votes, not by better purchases.

studies.caveats: Field evidence is correlational and from a single platform in one country (JD.com); membership is self-selected, so happier customers may both join and rate higher. Supporting experiments were lab-based.

items.title: A smiley face on the snack wrapper makes dieters guess it has more calories
items.angle: A fun food-packaging line: across five experiments, smiling faces on indulgent foods made people see them as more of a treat, which raised their calorie estimates. The effect was strongest in people actively watching what they eat, and it made them less likely to pick the item.
items.why_now: Online for 12 days (verified), not covered.
items.is_it_real: These were experiments measuring perceptions and stated choices, probably on online panels, not real purchases. Sample sizes and country aren't in the abstract. It applies only to foods that can read as indulgent.

studies.caveats: Experimental studies, likely online panels, with perceptions and choice measures rather than real retail purchases; effect is specific to foods that can be construed as indulgent; sample sizes and country not specified in the abstract.

items.title: 41,000 dogs: mixed breeds outlived purebreds of the same size, and dog deaths tracked human deaths state by state
items.angle: A light item from the Dog Aging Project: median lifespan ran from about 14 years for small dogs to under 10 for giant breeds. Females outlived males, AKC purebreds lived slightly shorter lives than mixed breeds of the same size, and regional dog mortality followed human mortality.
items.why_now: Online for 1 day (verified), not covered.
items.is_it_real: Owner-reported deaths in a self-selected volunteer cohort. The purebred gap was modest, and the 804-variable scan generates hypotheses only. This is a dog study, so none of it applies to people.

studies.caveats: This is a dog study, not a human one; findings about aging in dogs cannot be applied to people. Deaths and health exposures were owner-reported, the cohort is a self-selected volunteer sample of engaged pet owners, and the survey-wide association scan is hypothesis-generating only — the authors explicitly call for causal follow-up.

items.title: Signing up for DashPass or Postmates Unlimited was linked to nearly double the spending on that app, without cutting what people spent elsewhere
items.angle: The delivery membership isn't so much a discount as a habit machine. Spending on the subscribed app rose about 90% with no average drop at rival apps, though transaction data can only show a link.
items.why_now: Online 9 days in the Journal of Marketing Research, and the holiday delivery-subscription promos are coming.
items.is_it_real: Individual-level transaction data analyzed with a matched difference-in-differences design. That reduces, but cannot remove, the bias that heavy orderers are the ones who subscribe. The 90.4% figure is for the combined data, not Postmates alone. The data come from an early, partly pre-COVID platform era. Don't promise readers they'll keep spending more after cancelling; the fact-check flagged that as an overreach.

studies.caveats: Observational transaction data from two U.S. platforms in one category; difference-in-differences with matching reduces but cannot fully eliminate selection into subscribing; effects are associations, and the pre-COVID/early-platform era may not generalize to today's market.

items.title: Shoppers who couldn't use search filters browsed wider and picked pricier headphones
items.angle: Filters don't just reveal what you want, they shape it. Shoppers on a site with filters restricted explored more and ended up paying more and choosing more varied products. That's a quick, counterintuitive line about how online store design steers your basket.
items.why_now: Online 6 days in Marketing Science, ahead of holiday online shopping.
items.is_it_real: A randomized, incentive-aligned experiment with 1,200 online panelists on a store the researchers built. It covered one product category (wireless headphones) in a single session. It's a good lab-to-life hint, not proof that real retailers' filters cost you money.

studies.caveats: Online panel participants on a researcher-built platform, single product category (headphones), single shopping session; incentive-aligned but not a real retail environment.

items.title: The chatbot that gushes 'Great question!' over your refund status is doing it wrong, and friendlier medical intake bots don't get people to open up about embarrassing problems
items.angle: Two new experiment sets say warmth and personalization from a bot help only in some situations. Cheerful tone helped on taste-based tasks but hurt on factual ones. Personalized pre-visit medical chatbots raised willingness to disclose only for low-stigma conditions.
items.why_now: Both online within the last 12 days. Brands and health systems are rolling out chatbots with a single 'friendly' voice.
items.is_it_real: Both are scenario experiments measuring satisfaction or stated willingness to disclose, not real conversations. The tone study used three experiments with 587 people plus Weibo posts, in a Chinese context. The health-bot study's sample sizes and country aren't given, and its confirming field survey is cross-sectional. Keep it in a clause: 'in scenario experiments'.

studies.caveats: Scenario experiments rather than real service encounters; 587 participants across three studies means modest cell sizes; Chinese context and commercial text-based service only; satisfaction was the sole outcome, with no repurchase or word-of-mouth measures.

studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.caveats: Scenario experiments with stated disclosure intentions rather than observed disclosure; the confirmatory study is a cross-sectional survey that cannot establish causation; sample sizes and country not specified in the abstract.

items.title: People buy for their pets the way they buy for themselves: wellness shoppers get the healthy kibble, treat buyers get the treats
items.angle: Nearly 876,000 supermarket baskets show 'pet-owner synchrony': shoppers who buy healthy or indulgent products for themselves tend to buy the matching kind for their pets on the same trip. It's a fun, relatable one-liner.
items.why_now: Online 12 days in the Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science; pet spending is a perennial consumer story.
items.is_it_real: Scanner data from one regional US supermarket chain (875,853 baskets). Pet ownership is inferred from purchases, and items appearing in the same basket is correlation, not evidence of a psychological motive. It works as a quirky stat, not a finding about why.

studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
studies.caveats: One regional supermarket chain in a single country; basket co-occurrence is correlational and pet ownership is inferred from purchases rather than observed; no causal test of the proposed psychological mechanism.

items.title: Start the workday thinking about what went right: in a 10-day randomized study, replaying errors made workers less willing to try new things
items.angle: This complicates the 'learn from your mistakes' journaling advice. Morning reflection on errors cut exploration through lower attentiveness and more shame, and status-driven employees were hit hardest. Reflecting on successes did the opposite.
items.why_now: An evergreen productivity-advice counterpoint; online 55 days, so it suits the roundup, not a pitch.
items.is_it_real: A randomized experience-sampling field experiment, but small: 102 full-time employees over 10 workdays. Behavior was self-reported each day, and long-term learning wasn't measured. The country isn't stated in the abstract.

studies.caveats: Single study with 102 employees over 10 workdays; outcomes are self-reported daily behavior; short time horizon means long-term learning effects are unknown; sample and national context not fully specified in the abstract.

items.title: When a hospital asks a court for guardianship over an older patient, it almost always gets it, and poorer patients get strangers and fuller control
items.angle: Courts granted 99% of hospital-filed guardianship petitions that were heard. Medicaid recipients were less likely to get a guardian who knew them, and less-educated patients were more often put under full rather than limited guardianship. It's a sharp number on a process with little oversight.
items.why_now: Online 1 day in JAGS; guardianship and conservatorship abuse remains a live public concern.
items.is_it_real: A retrospective review of 236 petitions filed by one large academic health system in one county's probate court, 2019 to 2024. The subgroups are small, and the code blocks a pitch because the findings rest on subgroups. The 99% grant rate is descriptive and solid for this one system, but the Medicaid and education links are associations from one place. Say 'at one health system'.

studies.journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per subgroup), observational design, single-center, secondary analysis

items.title: Every 'hypoallergenic' vulvar soothing product in a 65-product US check contained a known skin allergen
items.angle: 'Natural', 'hypoallergenic' and 'fragrance-free' labels didn't predict a lower allergen load. 78% of products had at least one allergen, and 28% of 'fragrance-free' ones had botanical scent allergens. Plain ointments fared best, which gives readers a practical takeaway.
items.why_now: Online 7 days in Menopause, and 'clean' and 'gentle' labeling claims are under constant scrutiny.
items.is_it_real: A cross-sectional ingredient-list analysis of 65 over-the-counter products checked against an 80-allergen patch-test series. Containing an allergen is not the same as causing reactions, and no patients were tested. One author reports institutional funding from Galderma. It overlaps the existing menopause-site brief on vulvar itching (42817742) and the earlier 'gentle ingredients' pitch, so keep this to a single roundup line, and the brief can cite it.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, cross-sectional, industry funding [Galderma — institutional funding to one author]

items.title: Fewer than half of older Americans with probable dementia had a diagnosis in their Medicare records, and Medicare Advantage lagged behind Traditional Medicare
items.angle: In the latest years studied (2015 to 2019), adjusted detection was 48.8% in Traditional Medicare vs 39.2% in Medicare Advantage. Detection of early-stage dementia, when a diagnosis matters most, stayed flat. A useful line with a clock: the annual wellness visit includes a cognitive check.
items.why_now: Medicare open enrollment runs Oct 15 to Dec 7, when people are choosing between Traditional and Advantage plans.
items.is_it_real: A Yale analysis linking Health and Retirement Study surveys to Medicare claims for 3,144 people with probable dementia. Dementia status comes from a survey algorithm (Langa-Weir), not a clinical exam, and claims can miss diagnoses that were made but never coded. It can't say why the plan types differ. It overlaps the 10-25 pitch on early dementia signs being written off, so if that pitch lands, fold this number into it instead.

studies.caveats: Observational cohort study — cannot establish why detection differs by plan type; dementia status was determined by a survey-based algorithm (Langa-Weir), not clinical exam; claims data may miss diagnoses made but not coded.

items.title: At one Croatian hospital, the share of community C. diff cases that followed a dentist's antibiotic more than doubled in nine years, often clindamycin given without a penicillin allergy
items.angle: A useful prompt for readers: ask whether you really need an antibiotic for dental work, and why you're getting clindamycin if you aren't allergic to penicillin. Clindamycin is one of the antibiotics most tied to C. diff.
items.why_now: Online 7 days in Infection; antibiotic stewardship in dentistry is a recurring theme.
items.is_it_real: A retrospective study of 666 adults with community-acquired C. diff after outpatient antibiotics at one Croatian infectious-disease hospital, 2011 to 2019. The dental share rose from 13.1% to 31.1% (28.5% overall). The digest headline's 'nearly 1 in 3 dangerous gut infections' overstates it: these are only post-antibiotic community cases at one center, and Croatian prescribing may differ from US practice. Use 'at one hospital in Croatia'.

studies.caveats: single-center, observational design, single-region (Croatia — prescribing patterns may differ from US/UK dental practice), no sex-disaggregated data, retrospective design

items.title: How you drive, not how fast, flagged coming cognitive decline about 18 months before diagnosis in a small WashU study
items.angle: GPS trackers in older drivers' cars picked up changes in cornering and in how many different places people drove. Those changes came before a mild cognitive impairment diagnosis by a median of 18 months, with no gene or memory test needed. The useful idea for readers is that losing your 'range' (going to fewer places) may be an early sign worth noticing. The caveat fits in a clause: only 25 people actually declined.
items.why_now: Online 7 days ago (date verified) and not widely covered. Passive tracking and wearables for early dementia detection is a live consumer-tech topic.
items.is_it_real: It's an early signal, not a test. 298 older adults were followed, but only 25 progressed to impairment, all at a single center. The prediction accuracy (AUC 0.75) is moderate: useful in research, nowhere near diagnostic. It links driving changes to decline and doesn't show cause. The tie to the blood marker pTau217 was only 'directional'. The same WashU driving project has been covered before, which is why this is a roundup item and not a pitch. Say 'linked to' or 'flagged', never 'predicts Alzheimer's'.

studies.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Series B
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 progressors — only 25 converters), single-center, short follow-up relative to disease timeline

items.title: Baking soda with a carb-heavy breakfast cut about 30 seconds off recreational women's 10K times, with no extra stomach trouble
items.angle: This is one of the rare sports-supplement trials run on recreational women runners instead of male athletes. Baking soda is an old trick that usually causes gut distress, but taken with a carb-rich meal 90 minutes before the run it gave about a 1% gain (32 seconds over roughly 51 minutes). Stomach symptoms were no worse than with placebo. The caveat: the dose is not 'a spoonful'.
items.why_now: Online 3 days ago (date verified). It fits the running thread of 'sports science is finally studying women', and fall race season is under way.
items.is_it_real: It's a properly run double-blind, randomized crossover trial, but small (21 women, one center in Türkiye, one race each way). The time gain was statistically significant but modest. The digest's 'spoonful' framing is wrong. The dose was 0.3 g per kg of body weight, several teaspoons for most women. By my own arithmetic (not from the paper), that is roughly 5 g of sodium for a 60 kg runner, about double the recommended daily limit. That matters for anyone with high blood pressure, and the item should say so. No one should try it for the first time on race day.

studies.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, study population from Türkiye

items.title: Spinal cord injury deaths have climbed since 2016 among Americans 55 to 74, and falls drive most of them in the oldest
items.angle: In 25 years of US death certificates, spinal cord injury deaths fell among young adults while they rose 43% to 60% among people 55 to 74 after 2016. Falls account for 59% of these deaths in people 85 and older. For readers, it's another number arguing for strength and balance work in midlife, not just in old age.
items.why_now: Online 3 days ago (date verified). With winter coming and ice-related falls ahead, it's a timely reason to bring up fall prevention.
items.is_it_real: The data are real and national (31,279 deaths from CDC WONDER). But this is ecological death-certificate data with no individual detail. It can't say why deaths rose, and changes in how deaths are coded could be part of it. Before the item runs, check whether the 43–60% rise is in age-specific rates or raw counts, since an aging population alone would raise counts. The reported disparities (men 3.59 times the rate of women, Black adults 1.75 times that of white adults) are rate ratios and should be described that way, not as 'times more likely'. Fall prevention already has two routed pitches, so this belongs as a short item, not a new pitch.

studies.journal: The Journal of Spinal Cord Medicine
studies.caveats: observational design, ecological study (CDC WONDER death records), no individual-level data

items.title: Kids who got a rare platelet disorder after their first MMR shot showed no added risk after the second
items.angle: Take: a large English study of hospital and vaccination records found MMR dose 1 carries a small ITP (low-platelet) risk, about 1 in 42,900 doses. Dose 2 carried no added risk, including in 336 children who had ITP after dose 1, so doctors don't need to stop the series. It's a timely, reassuring number during measles outbreaks.
items.why_now: Online 1 day ago, and measles outbreaks are in the news.
items.is_it_real: Self-controlled case series on national linked records, which is the standard design for vaccine-safety signals and a strong one. The dose-2 reassurance rests on 336 children, which is solid for a rare event but not huge. Give the absolute risk, not the 2.4-fold relative figure, as the headline number.

studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

items.title: The RSV antibody shot for babies protects strongly at first, then fades over the first year
items.angle: Take: as RSV season starts, Queensland's first year of nirsevimab was linked to 78% fewer RSV hospitalizations in the first month of life, falling to 23% by nine months and not significant after that. That's why timing the shot to the season matters.
items.why_now: US RSV season is starting now, and parents are deciding about infant RSV protection.
items.is_it_real: Population surveillance data from one Australian state, observational, comparing against earlier birth cohorts, so changes in testing or circulation could affect the numbers. The waning curve is the useful new detail. The headline 78% applies only to month one.

studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, short follow-up

items.title: Small doesn't mean safe: many melanomas under 6 mm were already invasive
items.angle: Take: the 'bigger than a pencil eraser' rule misses things. In 160 confirmed melanomas 6 mm or smaller, 42.5% were already invasive, only 30% showed three or more ABCDE warning signs, and the ABCDE score didn't predict which were invasive. Dermoscopy checks caught more of them early.
items.why_now: Online 9 days ago, not covered. It's an easy, useful skin-check item.
items.is_it_real: Retrospective study from Spain of lesions already confirmed as melanoma. It does NOT mean half of small moles are dangerous, which is the trap in the digest headline. It means that among small melanomas, many had already invaded. No skin-tone or sex breakdown. The item must say that in a clause.

studies.caveats: observational design, retrospective, no sex-disaggregated data, single-region (Spain)

items.title: Water workouts, tai chi and wall sits ranked near the top for lowering blood pressure in a 284-trial analysis
items.angle: Take: for anyone whose knees rule out jogging, a network meta-analysis of 284 trials (18,750 adults with high or borderline blood pressure) ranked aquatic exercise first for lowering systolic pressure (about 10 mmHg), mind-body exercise first for diastolic, and isometric holds as efficient at modest weekly doses.
items.why_now: Online 9 days ago, not covered. It's useful and counter to the 'just walk more' default.
items.is_it_real: Large pool of randomized trials, but the rankings are indirect estimates across very different trials, not head-to-head tests. Mean age is 57, so frail older adults are underrepresented, and the dose figures are modeled. Say 'ranked highest in pooled trials', not 'beats the gym'.

studies.caveats: Network meta-analysis pools trials that differ widely in design, supervision and participant characteristics, so head-to-head rankings are estimates rather than direct comparisons. Mean age was 56.8 years, so the oldest and frailest adults are likely underrepresented. Dose-response figures come from modelling, not from trials that directly tested those doses.

items.title: The '30% rule' for diversity: a review of 277 studies finds a tipping point around 29%
items.angle: The idea behind campaigns like the 30% Club is that a group has to reach a critical mass before it changes anything. Among studies designed well enough to test that, 83% found a threshold, averaging about 29% representation. Caveat in a clause: it is a vote count of mostly correlational studies, not a pooled estimate.
items.why_now: A tidy number on a long-running debate about boards and teams. At 45 days old, it is too stale for a pitch.
items.is_it_real: An integrative review, not a meta-analysis with pooled effects. About a third of studies couldn't test the idea at all, and publication bias could inflate support. The 29% average hides wide variation. The underlying studies show links, not causes.

studies.caveats: This is a conceptual review and vote-count-style synthesis of published studies, not a new meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes, so publication bias and the heavy exclusion of methodologically weak studies could inflate the apparent support. The 29% average masks wide variation across settings, outcomes and which group is underrepresented, and most underlying studies are correlational — crossing a threshold is associated with better outcomes, not proven to cause them (better-performing organizations may simply be more able to reach critical mass).

items.title: The 'Liquid Death' problem: ironic brand names make healthy products seem less healthy
items.angle: In a set of experiments, joke or transgressive names lowered how moral a product seemed, and that dragged down how healthy it seemed. The effect held for smoothies but not milkshakes, and a clear nutrition label on the pack softened it. Caveat: lab ratings, not sales.
items.why_now: Online 12 days, uncovered. Edgy challenger-brand names are everywhere in the drinks and snack aisle.
items.is_it_real: Lab experiments measuring perceptions and purchase intention. The abstract gives no sample sizes or country. Edgy names did not reliably raise purchase intention either. Fictitious brands can't reproduce real brand equity.

studies.caveats: Lab-style experiments measuring perceptions and purchase intentions rather than observed sales; abstract does not report sample sizes, recruitment source or country; real-world brands like Liquid Death carry brand equity that fictitious stimuli cannot replicate.

items.title: When Aldi or Lidl starts carrying a big brand, rival supermarkets tend to cut its price
items.angle: More than 300 cases in three European grocery markets show conventional supermarkets cutting prices on national brands after a discounter listed them. The listings actually raised the supermarkets' sales of those brands. Caveat: European data, and whether the cuts paid off varied by brand.
items.why_now: Grocery prices remain a political issue, and Aldi is still expanding in the US.
items.is_it_real: Observational market data covering short-run sales only. The fact-check flags that the digest's 'most cuts don't pay off' line leaves out the abstract's finding that cuts on average improved sales. Keep the roundup line to the price-cut pattern. The publication date has not been verified.

studies.caveats: Observational market data rather than a randomized experiment; three European grocery markets and leading HiLo retailers only; focuses on short-run sales effects, so longer-term brand or traffic consequences of price moves are not captured.

items.title: Exercise, alcohol, medications and even your period can make an allergic reaction more severe
items.angle: Nearly 17,000 cases in the European Anaphylaxis Registry: medication was the most common cofactor in adults (41%), then exercise (27%). Menstruation was suspected in 4% of adult cases. More cofactors at once went with worse reactions and a later start of symptoms after eating a trigger food. Caveat: cofactors were suspected, not proven.
items.why_now: Online 2 days, uncovered, with a useful takeaway for anyone carrying an epinephrine auto-injector.
items.is_it_real: A large registry, but it is observational and cofactors were judged by suspicion. It describes how often cofactors appear, not how much each raises risk. European population.

studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, European registry population (may not generalize globally), cofactor data based on suspicion rather than confirmed causation

items.title: In later life, mood matters as much as blood pressure: two quarter-million-person studies link low mood combos to dementia and disability
items.angle: In about 247,000 Dutch adults, the late-life group combining loneliness, depression and inactivity had the highest dementia risk of any risk-factor group (hazard ratio 1.23). In about 258,000 adults across six international aging studies, low mood plus poor word recall was linked to roughly double the risk of needing help with daily tasks (RR 2.19). Caveat: both observational, effects modest.
items.why_now: Both online within 3 days, both uncovered. Paired, they make one useful item.
items.is_it_real: Very large cohorts, but observational with self-reported risk factors. The dementia hazard ratios are modest. Cognition was measured with one word-recall task. They show links, not causes. Say 'linked to.'

studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish that these clusters cause dementia; risk factors were largely self-reported in a single survey wave; Dutch population may not generalize elsewhere; hazard ratios are modest in size.

Observational pooled cohort data — it cannot show that depression or memory decline causes disability; depressive symptoms were self-reported and cognition was measured with a single word-recall task; mortality hazards were nonproportional; the harmonized cohorts differ in measurement and culture, so findings may not translate evenly to every population.

items.title: Lecanemab outside trials: brain-swelling risk is about one in three for people with two APOE4 copies
items.angle: Pooled data from 37 real-world studies: about 15% of patients overall had brain swelling or small bleeds (ARIA). The rate was 34% with two APOE4 copies versus 11% with none, and 23% versus 11.5% with or without existing microbleeds. US rates ran about double Asian rates. Caveat: there were no control groups, so these studies can't show cognitive benefit.
items.why_now: Online 4 days, uncovered. Families weighing infusions can get both answers (genotype and MRI) before the first dose.
items.is_it_real: A meta-analysis of uncontrolled observational cohorts with substantial heterogeneity and follow-up of 12 months or less. The risk numbers are useful and broadly match the trials. Nothing here speaks to whether the drug works.

studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of observational real-world cohorts with no control arms, so cognitive outcomes cannot be interpreted as efficacy; substantial heterogeneity between regions; overlapping patient cohorts across included studies required statistical adjustment; follow-up largely 12 months or less.

items.title: The first vaccine for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a tick-borne virus, passed its first human safety test
items.angle: An Oxford-style adenovirus-vector vaccine against a WHO priority virus that kills up to 40% of people it infects was well tolerated in 46 UK adults and produced antibodies after two doses. Caveat: phase 1 safety only, years from use.
items.why_now: Online 2 days in Lancet Infectious Diseases and not covered. It is a first-in-human milestone.
items.is_it_real: Phase 1: small, open-label, not randomized, single center, short follow-up. It shows safety and an immune response, not protection. Too early for a pitch unless a climate-and-ticks story gives it a stake.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), open-label, non-randomised, single-center, short follow-up

items.title: GLP-1 hair shedding is far more common in real life than trials reported, tied to how fast you lose weight, and usually temporary
items.angle: A review of trial, real-world and pharmacovigilance data says hair loss on semaglutide and tirzepatide is mostly telogen effluvium driven by rapid weight loss, not drug toxicity. It's most likely in women and in people who lose more than 10% of body weight, and it's usually reversible. Caveat in a clause: it's a narrative review, and the 'over 70%' real-world figure needs its source checked.
items.why_now: Online 11 days. 'Managing weight loss after glp-1' is exploding in this week's searches.
items.is_it_real: Thin to moderate. It's a narrative, not systematic, review, and some of the source data is self-reported. The gap between 3–7% in trials and over 70% in real-world reports probably reflects how differently each setting counted shedding. The roundup should not print 70% without checking where it came from.

studies.caveats: observational design, narrative review (not systematic), self-reported outcomes in some source studies

items.title: After gestational diabetes, lifestyle programs in the next five years cut type 2 diabetes risk
items.angle: An updated living meta-analysis (25 studies, 7,379 women) found mainly-lifestyle interventions within five years of a gestational-diabetes pregnancy lowered type 2 diabetes risk: risk ratio about 15% lower, hazard ratio about 32% lower. Caveat in a clause: the interventions varied a lot, and there's little data on drugs.
items.why_now: Online 13 days. It's a usable number for the roughly 1 in 7 pregnancies affected worldwide.
items.is_it_real: Moderate. It's a meta-analysis that includes randomized studies, but the interventions differ widely. Report the two effect measures separately and by type (RR 0.85, HR 0.68), not as 'a third'.

studies.caveats: secondary analysis, heterogeneous interventions across included studies, predominantly lifestyle interventions with limited pharmacotherapy data, multinational study populations with varying baseline risk

items.title: Your vitamin D pill probably isn't preventing frailty unless you're actually low, and big once-in-a-while doses have been linked to more falls
items.angle: A review of cohort studies and RCTs finds that trials in adults with adequate vitamin D levels mostly came up neutral for frailty. Intermittent high-dose 'bolus' regimens were associated with more falls and fractures, and benefit seems limited to people who are deficient. Caveat in a clause: it's a narrative review, and the lead author has had funding from a vitamin D maker.
items.why_now: Vitamin D is among the most-taken supplements by older adults. The paper's date is unverified (about 17 days), so confirm it's within the roundup window.
items.is_it_real: Moderate. The conclusion matches earlier large trials, but this paper is a narrative review with an industry tie (Abiogen). It's useful as a service item, not new evidence.

studies.caveats: observational design, narrative review (not systematic meta-analysis), industry funding [Abiogen — prior research funding to lead author]

items.title: Breastfeeding longer and more exclusively was linked to less postpartum weight hanging on through the first year
items.angle: A quick, usable answer to a question new parents search all the time. In 714 Chinese mothers followed to 12 months, more cumulative breastfeeding was linked to lower odds of ending up on a high or moderate weight-retention path, and exclusive early breastfeeding looked best. Caveat in a clause: it's observational, so mothers who breastfeed longer may differ in other ways.
items.why_now: Online 13 days (verified), inside the roundup window, and not widely covered.
items.is_it_real: Observational cohort in one country, so confounding (income, sleep, return to work) is likely and the result is an association, not proof breastfeeding causes weight loss. Funded by Danone Nutricia, a formula maker, which would if anything cut against a pro-breastfeeding result. Moderate sample, four time points, trajectory modeling.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country cohort (China — generalizability to other populations uncertain), industry funding [Danone Nutricia], self-reported breastfeeding mode possible

items.title: A bleeding disorder twice as common as hemophilia, and worst for women, has no approved drug, but six are now in trials
items.angle: HHT causes frequent nosebleeds, anemia and hidden blood-vessel malformations that can lead to stroke. The review calls it the most damaging inherited bleeding disorder in women and counts six drug candidates in clinical development. One line with the caveat: these are early trials, not treatments yet.
items.why_now: In The Lancet Haematology 14 days ago.
items.is_it_real: A review with no new trial data. Several authors have consulting or research ties to the companies developing the drugs. The prevalence (about 1 in 5,000) and the 'no licensed therapy' claim are well established. Pipeline drugs may fail.

studies.caveats: review article (no original trial data), industry funding [Agios, Atavistik, Sobi, Vaderis, Novartis, Amgen, Alnylam — author consulting and research relationships], surrogate endpoints only

items.title: Kids with selective mutism in Norway weren't diagnosed until about age 10 on average, and girls waited longer than boys
items.angle: A quick parent-useful item with an echo of ADHD in girls. In a national registry of 1,591 children, the average age at diagnosis was 10.1. Girls were referred and diagnosed later than boys. Half had another diagnosis, usually anxiety, and nearly a third got medication, mostly SSRIs in adolescence.
items.why_now: Online 16 days, inside the roundup window. Girls being diagnosed later echoes the women-and-ADHD conversation she already writes about.
items.is_it_real: National registry data covering all specialist-care cases in Norway, so it's population-wide but only one health system. The digest headline 'years too late' overstates it: the measured gap from referral to diagnosis is about one year. 'Years' would depend on typical onset age, which this summary doesn't give, so check the paper before using it. The size of the girl-boy gap isn't given here either; confirm it.

studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (Norway), registry-based (ICD-10 diagnoses only), self-reported (parent-reported) outcomes not applicable — clinical registry data

items.title: A video e-consult model let pediatricians finish toddler autism evaluations in a median 73 days
items.angle: Waits for autism evaluations often stretch for months. At Vanderbilt, trained primary care doctors recorded short diagnostic visits and sent the videos to psychologists, who all replied within a week. Median time from first concern to finished e-consult was 73 days, and the pediatricians' impressions largely matched the specialists'.
items.why_now: Online 19 days and not widely covered. Long waits for autism diagnosis are a common pain point for parents.
items.is_it_real: 81 children at one health system, with no comparison group. The design shows the model works there, not that it beats usual care. The caveat fits in a clause: small, single-site, no head-to-head with standard referral.

studies.journal: Journal of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design, short follow-up, narrow age range

items.title: A clear ultrasound doesn't rule out endometriosis
items.angle: At one Australian hospital, specialised ultrasound found ovarian endometriosis cysts about 81% of the time but rarely spotted the peritoneal disease that also drives pain. If your scan was 'normal' and the pain isn't, that's not the end of the conversation.
items.why_now: Online about 17 days by the digest's date, inside the roundup window. Confirm the date.
items.is_it_real: Retrospective review of 221 patients at one hospital who went on to surgery, so the sample leans toward people suspected of having disease. The finding fits what specialists already know about ultrasound's limits, which makes it a useful reminder rather than a discovery.

studies.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, retrospective cohort, study population in Australia, short follow-up not applicable (diagnostic study)

items.title: For many autistic adults, a deep special interest works as a way to manage emotions, and the stigma around it is the cost
items.angle: A German survey compared 60 autistic adults with 122 non-autistic adults. The autistic group leaned on their intense interests to manage stress more than they sought out people, and they also got more negative reactions about those interests. It's a quick reframe: the interest may be a coping tool, not just a symptom to manage.
items.why_now: Online about 19 days. 'Signs of autistic burnout in adults' is exploding in Trend Desk searches this week.
items.is_it_real: This is a self-reported online survey from one country with only 60 autistic participants, and the online date isn't verified. It shows what people say about how they use their interests, not measured emotional outcomes. That's fine for a single roundup line with the caveat in a clause, and not enough for more.

studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, WEIRD sample (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic), online survey, single-country (Germany)

items.title: Caffeine didn't help people tune out distractions in a lab test, only a small speed bump
items.angle: In three lab experiments at Texas A&M, 200 mg of caffeine (about two cups of coffee) didn't improve how well people filtered distractions or picked up visual patterns. The only gain was slightly faster target detection, in one of the three experiments. Short and useful, with the caveat in a clause: small lab study.
items.why_now: Online 4 days (verified). It pairs with the clocks falling back on Nov 1, when people reach for more coffee.
items.is_it_real: Thin but honest if framed narrowly. The sample was small (under 100), the design single-blind rather than double-blind, at one university, using computer visual-search tasks. It tested selective attention, not alertness, reaction time when sleep-deprived, or mood, so it can't support 'coffee doesn't help you focus' in general. Say 'in lab tests' and give no N, because the abstract count isn't in the digest.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-blind (not double-blind) design, single-center, no sex-disaggregated data, lab-based tasks may not reflect real-world attention demands

items.title: Over a decade with Parkinson's, psychosis and apathy climbed while anxiety eased
items.angle: In 846 people with biomarker-confirmed Parkinson's tracked for 10 years, the odds of psychosis rose about 21% per year and apathy about 17% per year, while anxiety dipped slightly. It's a useful heads-up for families on what to watch for as the disease progresses.
items.why_now: Trend Desk has Marshall Faulk's Parkinson's disclosure as a roundup item this week, so this could run next to it. The study has been online 19 days (verified).
items.is_it_real: A large, well-characterized cohort (PPMI), but observational. The effects are per-year odds ratios, not prevalence. The digest's 'psychosis nearly doubled' line isn't backed by the summary, so don't use it. The digest calls PPMI US-only, but it has international sites, so check before saying so.

studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (US) cohort

items.title: An ER visit for a fall can be an early warning sign of a first seizure
items.angle: Across 57,547 adults with a first seizure in 11 states, the odds of a fall-related ER visit in the week before the seizure were about 2.6 times the odds in the same week a year earlier. The signal stretched back as far as 22 weeks. Unexplained falls deserve a second look.
items.why_now: Recent (about 10 days, date unverified; confirm it's within the 21-day roundup window). It's a practical, quick takeaway for readers and caregivers.
items.is_it_real: A case-crossover design using administrative ER data. That's a reasonable method, but the figure is an odds ratio, not 'times more likely', and it only covers the 7,307 people who had a prior fall visit. Mean age was 49, so it's not an older-adult finding. Some 'falls' may have been unrecognized seizures, which supports the point rather than undermining it.

studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, no age breakdown reported, mean age 49.3 years (older adult subgroup not separately analyzed)

items.title: Six minutes of daily stretching eased fibromyalgia symptoms in a small six-week trial
items.angle: A useful, quick number. A home routine short enough to actually do improved fibromyalgia impact scores by about 19%, and adherence was 83%. That's relevant for a condition where high-intensity exercise often backfires.
items.why_now: Online about 17 days (unverified). It's an RCT with a takeaway readers can use.
items.is_it_real: Small RCT: 58 adults, six weeks, compared against a waitlist rather than a placebo or attention control, with self-reported outcomes. The authors flag a sex imbalance. The caveat clause: small, short, and unblinded. Confirm the online date before it runs.

studies.journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), short follow-up, waitlist-controlled (not placebo-controlled), self-reported outcomes, sex imbalance noted by authors

items.title: $200+ smart swim goggles didn't make swimmers any faster than the same workouts without them
items.angle: In a 12-week randomized trial of 57 recreational swimmers, real-time-feedback goggles (FORM) did no better than following the same training plan without them. Both groups improved swim speed by about 6–7%. The plan did the work, not the gadget.
items.why_now: Online 19 days. It's a quick, useful consumer-tech line that fits a Friday 'save your money' item.
items.is_it_real: This was a real RCT, but small and at a single center, with only 12 weeks of follow-up. A null result in 57 people can't rule out a small benefit. The roundup line should say 'no measurable edge', not 'useless'. Check whether FORM had any role in the study.

studies.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up

items.title: Your afternoon snack was linked to a bigger blood-sugar bump than a morning one, and moving for half an hour afterward blunted it
items.angle: 785 adults without diabetes wore glucose monitors and activity trackers for nine days. Afternoon and early-evening snacks produced larger glucose rises than morning ones, even after accounting for what was eaten, and moderate-to-vigorous activity in the 30 minutes after was linked to smaller rises. A useful line for the glucose-spike crowd.
items.why_now: Online 18 days (verified), and CGMs for people without diabetes are a live wellness trend.
items.is_it_real: Observational, Singapore only, self-reported food. The outcome is two-hour glucose area under the curve, not health outcomes. Nobody has shown that snack-level glucose bumps matter for people without diabetes.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country cohort (Singapore), self-reported dietary intake, no clinical outcomes beyond glucose iAUC

items.title: A Mediterranean lifestyle was linked to 30% lower death risk across every income and education level, and higher earners saw the biggest gap
items.angle: 105,812 Dutch adults followed for 13 years. The highest adherence to a Mediterranean diet-plus-lifestyle score (food, activity, rest, social habits) was linked to 30% lower all-cause mortality. Income amplified the association more than education did, which is a quiet hint that money matters more than knowing what to eat.
items.why_now: Online 16 days (verified). The disparity angle is the twist on a familiar diet story.
items.is_it_real: Observational. Self-reported diet scored once at baseline, Dutch cohort. HR 0.70 is a relative figure. The 46%-lower figure for high income plus high adherence compares against a reference group that mixes income and adherence, so frame the income point as suggestive.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported dietary intake, Dutch cohort (may not generalize globally), MEDLIFE scored at baseline only

items.title: ARFID isn't just picky eating: across 84 studies, about 44% of kids with it also had an anxiety disorder and nearly a third had nutritional deficiencies
items.angle: A meta-analysis putting numbers on how medically and psychiatrically tangled the 'picky eating disorder' is. GI disorders in 30%, nutritional deficiencies in 32%, anxiety in 44%, autism in 19%. Useful for parents who've seen ARFID on TikTok.
items.why_now: Online 21 days (verified, the last day roundup-eligible). ARFID awareness keeps rising online.
items.is_it_real: Pooled prevalence from mostly clinical samples, which skew toward sicker kids. Heterogeneity is high, publication bias was detected, and GRADE certainty is very low to low. Present the figures as rough estimates.

studies.caveats: observational design, high heterogeneity (I²≥75%), publication bias detected for anxiety/depression/nutritional deficiencies, very low to low GRADE certainty of evidence

items.title: Childhood abuse was linked to chronic constipation decades later in a large Harvard-affiliated cohort
items.angle: A gut-brain item. Gastroenterology adds chronic constipation to the list of gut conditions tied to early-life adversity, which suggests some stubborn constipation may not be a fiber problem.
items.why_now: Online 17 days (verified), in a top GI journal, and not widely covered.
items.is_it_real: The digest worked from the title and affiliations only; the abstract wasn't available. Before this runs, pull the paper for the cohort name, N and the odds ratio, and report it as an odds ratio. Abuse history is self-reported and recalled, and the design is observational. If the effect is small, cut it.

studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported dietary intake, self-reported abuse history, no mechanistic data, sample size not confirmed in abstract

items.title: Most Pokémon packs and Labubu blind boxes don't tell you your odds of a rare pull
items.angle: Researchers checked 50 trading card packs and blind boxes. 80% gave no odds at all, and not one let a buyer work out the chance of getting a specific card. That matters for products sold to kids with no age limit.
items.why_now: Online 13 days (verified). The Labubu and Pokémon card frenzies keep these products in the news.
items.is_it_real: The sample is small (50 packs) and all from Hong Kong, so the US shelf may differ. The study describes packaging and measures no harm to kids. The idea that this may break consumer law is the authors' argument, not a ruling. Add the caveat in a clause.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, WEIRD sample (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic)

items.title: Tourists left antibiotics in the soil of one of Earth's most remote mountaintops, even far from the campsites
items.angle: A weird-stat item. On Roraima-tepui, a 'sky island' above the Amazon with no sanitation, researchers found 11 pharmaceuticals including ciprofloxacin, some in zones visitors don't use. Caveat in a clause: resistance genes weren't measured.
items.why_now: Online 18 days (verified). It works for this Friday's roundup.
items.is_it_real: Soil chemistry from one site. The detections are real, but the antimicrobial-resistance risk is a modelled estimate, not measured resistance.

studies.caveats: observational design, single-center

items.title: A second kissing-bug species in the Southwest has been caught carrying the Chagas parasite
items.angle: Surveillance on military bases near the US-Mexico border in California and Arizona found the Chagas parasite in 9% of Paratriatoma hirsuta bugs, the first confirmation in wild-caught insects of this species, and in 7% of the better-known Triatoma rubida. Kissing bugs are a recurring viral scare, so a short, accurate item is useful.
items.why_now: Online 18 days with a verified date. Kissing-bug posts come back every year as viral fear content.
items.is_it_real: 83 insects collected from wood rat nests. This shows the parasite is present in the bugs. It does not show human infections. US-acquired Chagas is rare, and most US cases were acquired abroad. Put that in a clause.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-region (U.S.-Mexico border)

items.title: RSV shot for 60+: people on immune-suppressing drugs started with about nine times the hospitalization rate, and the vaccine appeared to protect them too
items.angle: In a 131,000-person Danish pragmatic trial, the RSV vaccine cut RSV hospitalizations in adults 60 and older by about 83%. Unvaccinated people with immunosuppression had about nine times the hospitalization rate of everyone else, which is the number readers on transplant, cancer or autoimmune drugs can use. Caveat in a clause: Pfizer funded it, and the immunosuppressed estimate is very imprecise.
items.why_now: RSV season is starting, and the study is 19 days old.
items.is_it_real: The overall effectiveness comes from a large randomized trial, but it was open-label, and only 21 RSV hospitalizations occurred, so the subgroup estimate is very imprecise (its interval crosses zero). Pfizer makes the vaccine and employs some of the authors. The fact-check flagged minor issues, so the item should use the abstract's numbers exactly.

studies.caveats: Funded by Pfizer, which manufactures RSVpreF, and several Pfizer employees are co-authors. Open-label with no placebo. Only 21 RSV hospitalizations occurred in total, so the immunosuppressed subgroup estimate is very imprecise and the trial was not powered to detect subgroup differences. Danish population may not generalize everywhere.

items.title: A non-hormonal hot-flash drug cut night waking at 4 weeks, but the sleep benefit was gone by week 12
items.angle: In a 110-woman trial, Bayer's elinzanetant cut about 22 minutes of night waking versus placebo at four weeks, measured in a sleep lab. By week 12 the gap was under a minute. A useful reality check for anyone asked to choose a non-hormonal menopause drug for sleep. Caveat in a clause: small, Bayer-funded, and the favorable whole-period results were post hoc.
items.why_now: Online 12 days, while menopause and perimenopause searches are exploding this week.
items.is_it_real: A randomized but small phase II trial (110 women, 12 weeks) funded and partly authored by Bayer. The prespecified week-12 comparison was null; the analyses favoring the drug were post hoc. Women were 40 to 65. The item should check elinzanetant's current US approval status before naming a brand.

studies.caveats: Small N (110), short 12-week follow-up, and industry funded — multiple authors are employees of Bayer, which develops elinzanetant. The favorable across-the-period findings came from post hoc analyses, not the prespecified comparison, and the primary objective measure showed no group difference at week 12. Participants were aged 40–65, so results may not generalize to women over 65.

items.title: Exercise alone in midlife wasn't linked to less cognitive impairment; exercise plus diet, no smoking and a healthy weight was
items.angle: A quick 'one habit isn't a shield' item. In 18 years of data on 3,011 British civil servants who were 45 to 64 at the start, the analysis simulated a trial. Starting or keeping up exercise on its own didn't significantly lower the risk of cognitive impairment. Bundling it with diet, not smoking and a normal BMI did, and adding blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar control did most. Caveat in a clause: a statistical emulation, not a real trial.
items.why_now: Online 14 days. Brain-health and dementia searches are running high this week.
items.is_it_real: Observational cohort data run through a target-trial emulation, so this is association, not causation. Whitehall II is British civil servants. Impairment was defined by test scores, not diagnosis. The fact-check flagged minor issues. Say 'wasn't linked to', not 'doesn't work'.

studies.caveats: Observational cohort with statistical emulation of a trial, not an actual randomized trial — causation cannot be established. Whitehall II is a cohort of British civil servants and may not generalize to other populations; cognitive impairment was defined by cognitive testing rather than clinical diagnosis.

items.title: Laser/light therapy added nothing to back-pain exercise in a fully blinded trial with a year of follow-up
items.angle: Red-light and laser therapy is sold everywhere, from clinics to home panels. In a 148-person trial where patients, therapists and assessors were all blinded, adding photobiomodulation to a back-exercise program changed pain by 0.4 points out of 10, and had no meaningful effect on disability or an inflammation marker, at any point up to 12 months. The exercise did the work. Caveat in a clause: one device and protocol, tested only as an add-on, in adults under 65.
items.why_now: Online 13 days. Red-light therapy is a steady consumer trend.
items.is_it_real: A well-blinded randomized trial with long follow-up. Limits: one device and dosing protocol, an add-on design (it doesn't test light therapy alone), and ages 18 to 65. The fact-check flagged minor issues. It says nothing about red light for skin or other uses, so the item shouldn't generalize past back pain.

studies.caveats: Participants were aged 18 to 65, so results cannot be assumed to apply to adults over 65 with chronic back pain; the trial tested one specific device and dosing protocol; it addresses photobiomodulation only as an add-on to exercise, not as a standalone therapy.

items.title: When a city hospital closes, older, uninsured and Medicaid patients absorb most of the damage
items.angle: A review of 24 US studies spanning six decades found urban hospital closures cluster in poorer, more diverse neighborhoods. They are followed by longer travel and waits, lost emergency and specialty access, and broken continuity of care. The harm falls hardest on elderly, uninsured, Medicaid and minority residents. Effects on deaths were mixed.
items.why_now: The authors warn that expected federal Medicaid cuts could speed up closures. It's a policy item with a take, found 21 days ago.
items.is_it_real: A systematic review of observational and qualitative studies (1961–2024), so it can't establish cause. The mortality findings were mixed, which belongs in the item. US urban settings only. One author has consulting ties. The online date hasn't been verified.

studies.caveats: Systematic review of observational and qualitative studies spanning six decades; cannot establish causation; findings on mortality were mixed and heterogeneous; U.S. urban settings only; one author reports consulting and grant relationships including Merck & Co. and federal technology policy offices.

items.title: Women's sleep doesn't shrink at midlife, it breaks up: 3.8 million smartwatch nights
items.angle: Smartwatch data from 192,500 women showed total sleep barely changed with age. But time awake after first falling asleep rose 15% at 50–54, 25% at 55–59 and 32% at 60–64, compared with women in their early 20s. Men's rose less. Caveat in a clause: the study was funded and largely written by Bayer and Samsung.
items.why_now: Online 12 days. It speaks to the menopause sleep complaint that keeps showing up in searches, and to the extra hour when clocks fall back Nov 1 (Trend Desk roundup).
items.is_it_real: A huge sample, but cross-sectional: it compares age groups rather than following the same women. Wearables estimate sleep rather than measure it, and smartwatch owners skew healthier and wealthier. Most authors work for Bayer (which sells a menopause drug) or Samsung. Report it as wake time after first falling asleep, not 'less sleep'.

studies.caveats: Cross-sectional comparison of age groups, not the same women followed over time, so it cannot show change within individuals. Consumer wearables estimate rather than directly measure sleep stages. Smartwatch owners are likely healthier and more affluent than the general population, and the upper age limit was 65. The study was conducted and funded by Bayer AG with Samsung Electronics; most authors are employees of one or the other.

items.title: 7,000 steps a few days a week was linked to better bones before menopause, not after
items.angle: In 3,529 Japanese women tracked with pedometers for about 3.5 years, hitting 7,000 steps on three or more days a week roughly halved the risk of a drop in bone quality, but only before menopause. After menopause, the link disappeared. Useful line for readers: keep walking for your heart and balance, but ask about strength or impact training for your bones.
items.why_now: Online 2 days. Walking is the default bone advice given to postmenopausal women.
items.is_it_real: Observational, with objective step counts (a plus). Bone was measured by heel ultrasound plus self-reported osteoporosis, not a DXA scan. One region of Japan, 3.5-year follow-up, minor fact-check flag. 'Linked to', not 'protects'.

studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation; bone status was assessed by quantitative ultrasound plus self-reported osteoporosis diagnosis rather than DXA; single-region Japanese population may not generalize; roughly 3.5-year follow-up.

items.title: Most people say the wrong thing to a friend with infertility, and knowing the facts doesn't help
items.angle: 72% of people picked at least one unhelpful response to a woman describing infertility, and knowing more about infertility made no difference. Useful line: information campaigns alone won't fix it.
items.why_now: Online 13 days, not widely covered, inside the roundup window.
items.is_it_real: An online vignette survey of 419 Canadian adults. It measures what people say they would say to an imagined woman, not real conversations. The association is real but limited to one country and self-report.

studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, online survey, vignette-based (hypothetical responses, not real interactions), single country (Canada)
